chunks.section: An Information Budget for Label-Noise Memorization, and What Statistical Complexity Tracks: A Study with Multilayer Perceptrons
chunks.text: Nancy Baygorrea C. nbaygorrea@gmail.com Affiliation: Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: State University of Northern Rio de Janeiro Otávio da Fonseca Martins Gomes ogomes@mn.ufrj.br Affiliation: Centre for Mineral Technology Affiliation: Postgraduate Program in Geosciences, Affiliation: National Museum, Rio de Janeiro

How much of a noisy training set has a network memorized, and when? We study this question for a multilayer perceptron and ask what a statistical complexity (entropy-disequilibrium) description of its predictions adds. Standard information identities decompose the information that the predictions carry about the inputs into signal, memorization ( I ⁡ ( Y ^ ; Y ~ ∣ Y ) I(\hat{Y};\tilde{Y}\mid Y) ) and heterogeneity terms. The memorization term is zero in the population for predictors that do not depend on the realized class-conditional noise. Fano’s inequality bounds it from below through training accuracies, but no upper bound follows from the memorized fraction M M . In 89 runs on MNIST with ten pre-specified hypotheses (five supported, four not supported, one not testable under the protocol), the normalized memorization term rose with M M on the training set, stayed near zero on held-out samples with freshly drawn noisy labels, and was close to its Fano bound. Unlike M M , it has no chance level by construction, although a chance correction of M M largely removed this difference. With every label replaced by an incorrect class, test accuracy fell to 0.5% while the predictions retained information about the true class. The peak of mean statistical complexity preceded memorization at corruption rates up to 40%; at higher rates it fell within the memorization phase, close to the epoch at which mean training confidence reached about 0.6, so the two could not be separated. As a stopping rule it matched established rules only at low noise, and it detected corrupted samples less well than simple label-free scores. Deep neural networks have been shown to fit training sets with randomly assigned labels ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . When exposed to partial label corruption, training often exhibits an early-learning pattern: models tend to learn consistent semantic structure before increasingly fitting corrupted labels ( Arpit et al., 2017 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , a behavior that has also been analyzed theoretically for gradient descent with early stopping ( Li et al., 2020b ) . Understanding this progression may help characterize generalization under label noise and inform early-stopping strategies ( Bai et al., 2021 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) . It also raises two research questions. RQ1: how much information about the label noise is reflected in a model’s predictions, and how does it relate to accuracy-based measures of memorization? RQ2: what do observable summaries of those predictions, in particular statistical complexity, track during training, and are they useful as stopping rules or as detectors of corrupted samples?

Several operational perspectives on memorization address different aspects of these questions. Counterfactual approaches, motivated by the role of memorization in learning long-tailed distributions ( Feldman, 2019 ) , assess memorization through the effect of including or removing individual examples from the training set ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Information-theoretic approaches examine the information that learned weights retain about label noise ( Harutyunyan et al., 2020 ) , or bound generalization through the mutual information ( Xu and Raginsky, 2017 ) or the conditional mutual information ( Steinke and Zakynthinou, 2020 ) between the training data and the output of a learning algorithm. Representation-based work reports that networks that memorize shuffled training labels can retain, in their internal layers, information that supports generalization to the true labels ( Ketha and Ramaswamy, 2026 ) . On the practical side, corrupted samples are often identified from training dynamics, for example through small losses ( Han et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020a ) , margins ( Pleiss et al., 2020 ) , forgetting events ( Toneva et al., 2019 ) or early-training error norms ( Paul et al., 2021 ) . Here, we work in function space, focusing on the classifier’s conditional predictive distributions p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) . We use the dependence between predictions and observed labels, conditional on the true class, as an operational measure of label-noise memorization, and investigate how this quantity relates to accuracy-based measures of label-noise fitting and to geometric summaries of the predictions.

Our geometric description draws on a statistical-physics framework that characterizes probability distributions through normalized Shannon entropy S S , disequilibrium 𝒟 \mathcal{D} relative to the uniform distribution, and statistical complexity 𝒞 = S ⋅ 𝒟 \mathcal{C}=S\cdot\mathcal{D} ( López-Ruiz et al., 1995 ; Martin et al., 2006 ; Rosso et al., 2007 ) . These quantities map each predictive distribution to a point in an admissible region of the ( S , 𝒟 ) (S,\mathcal{D}) plane, allowing its evolution to be followed during training. Because complexity vanishes at both the uniform and deterministic limits, it characterizes intermediate features of predictive geometry rather than directly measuring memorization. The order of aggregation also matters: computing statistics after averaging predictions can obscure differences among individual outputs. Confident predictions distributed across classes, for example, can have a nearly uniform mean despite having low per-sample entropy.

We therefore consider the mean per-sample complexity 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} and the within-group variance V V of per-sample complexity, with groups defined by the noisy label, as complementary descriptions of training dynamics. The former summarizes the complexity of individual predictive distributions, while the latter measures their dispersion within groups that mix clean and corrupted samples. To provide an information-theoretic reference, we consider a fixed trained model and define Y ^ \hat{Y} as a categorical variable sampled from p θ ( ⋅ ∣ X ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid X) . The entropy of the mean predictive distribution minus the mean per-sample entropy then equals I ⁡ ( X , Y ^ ) I(X;\hat{Y}) and with entropies normalized by ln ⁡ N \ln N for N N classes, the difference equals I ⁡ ( X , Y ^ ) / ln ⁡ N I(X;\hat{Y})/\ln N . This construction is similar in form to entropy-difference criteria used in Bayesian active learning ( Houlsby et al., 2011 ) , although the random variables and their interpretation differ. In the main grid of our experiments, the normalized entropy of the mean prediction remained above 0.99 0.99 , so marginal entropy alone offers limited separation between training regimes. Under the empirical distribution of the training set, the chain rule decomposes this predictive information exactly, without independence assumptions, into a signal term I ⁡ ( Y ^ , Y ) I(\hat{Y};Y) , a memorization term I ⁡ ( Y ^ ; Y ~ ∣ Y ) I(\hat{Y};\tilde{Y}\mid Y) and a heterogeneity term I ( Y ^ ; X ∣ Y , Y ~ ) I(\hat{Y};X\mid Y,\tilde{Y}) , where Y Y and Y ~ \tilde{Y} denote the clean and observed labels, respectively; the assumption of class-conditional noise is needed only to interpret the population value of the memorization term. This decomposition provides an information budget against which the geometric observables can be evaluated. Together with a Fano-type bound and an analysis of chance-level label matching, it helps distinguish the information associated with label-noise fitting from the predictive geometry summarized by statistical complexity.

Before the main runs, we specified ten hypotheses with decision criteria (Section 4 , Table 3 ). For RQ1, we expected the memorization term to exceed its permutation null on the training set but not on held-out samples (H2) and to agree with the memorized fraction (H3). For RQ2, we expected the peaks of V V and of a label-free heterogeneity term to fall within the memorization phase (H4); stopping at the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} to lose less test accuracy than simple baselines (H5); per-sample complexity to be non-inferior to established scores for detecting corrupted samples (H6); the ability of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} to distinguish noisy from clean runs to vanish after interpolation (H7); and the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} and the trajectories in the entropy-disequilibrium plane to be robust to the choice of functional, to temperature and to the seed (H9, H10). H8 concerns the differences between noise models at complete corruption, and H1 is an implementation check. None of the hypotheses specified what 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} tracks. The analysis of this question (Section 5.7 ) is exploratory and was motivated by the outcome of H4 and by the comparison of the H5 rule with established stopping rules.

This study is primarily empirical. Its theoretical component consists of standard identities and a Fano-type bound formulated for the setting considered here. We compute the signal, memorization and heterogeneity terms exactly for the empirical distribution defined by the logged predictions and the clean and noisy labels (Section 3 ). At the population level, the memorization term vanishes when the noisy label is conditionally independent of the input and the trained parameters given the clean class, and we give its value under complete memorization. To relate memorization information to the memorized fraction M M , the fraction of corrupted samples predicted with their noisy label, we derive a Fano-type lower bound on the normalized memorization term ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} in terms of training accuracies on clean and corrupted samples (Proposition 5 ). We also show that M = 0 M=0 is compatible with ℳ I = 1 \mathcal{M}_{I}=1 . In our runs, the bound was close to the observed ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} , suggesting that training accuracies accounted for much of its measured value. We further quantify the chance level of M M . A chance correction removed most of the resulting offset in estimated memorization times, while ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} has a zero population null under the stated independence condition (Section 5.5 ). We then examine what mean complexity tracked during training and assess its use as a practical tool. As a stopping rule, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} performed comparably to the established rules considered for ρ ≤ 0.4 \rho\leq 0.4 , but incurred substantially larger losses for ρ ≥ 0.6 \rho\geq 0.6 and was also outperformed under pair-flip noise. Finally, we examine differences among the noise models. Under complete UI corruption ( ρ = 1 \rho=1 ), every observed training label differs from the true class and is therefore a complementary label ( Ishida et al., 2017 ) . In our experiments, test predictions retained information about the true class despite below-chance accuracy. This contrasted with the results obtained under the two mechanisms that generate labels independently of the inputs, uniform resampling over all classes ( SU ) and permutation of the selected labels ( PERM ) (Section 5.6 ). The study comprises a main investigation on MNIST and an exploratory extension to Fashion-MNIST ( Xiao et al., 2017 ) , pair-flip noise ( Han et al., 2018 ) and four training variants (SGD, a cosine learning-rate schedule, weight decay and training for 400 epochs) (Sections 4 and 5.9 ), all with the same architecture. We report both supported and unsupported outcomes. Section 2 defines the noise models and the notation used throughout (Tables 1 and 2 ). We used MNIST ( LeCun et al., 1998 ) , comprising 60 000 training and 10 000 test images, with inputs standardized with a mean of 0.1307 and a standard deviation of 0.3081. The model was a 784 - 512 - 512 - 10 multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations, no dropout or weight decay, and 669 706 parameters. It was trained for 200 epochs using Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) , a constant learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , a batch size of 256, and cross-entropy loss on the noisy labels. Deterministic GPU settings were enabled. The label-noise seed was separate from the seed used for initialization and mini-batch ordering.

The grid comprised UI noise with ρ ∈ { 0 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 , 1 } \rho\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,1\} and 10 seeds per rate (60 runs); SU and PERM at ρ = 1 \rho=1 with 10 seeds each (20 runs); and a 3 × 3 3\times 3 design under UI noise at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 , crossing three noise realizations with three initialization seeds (9 runs). Training used PyTorch 2.6.0 (CUDA 12.4 build) on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU, with a mean wall-clock time of about 1.6-1.9 minutes per run.

The original algorithm evaluates prediction changes every n n training steps and we set this interval to one epoch. Because our settings of n n , k k and p p may differ from those of the original implementation, we report the full grid.

For rule selection, a family of 16 label-free rules was ranked using seeds { 42,123,456,789 , 101112 } \{42,123,456,789,101112\} according to their loss on the validation half of the test set. The selected rule was then evaluated on the evaluation half using the other five seeds. The family comprised arg ⁡ max ⁡ 𝒞 ¯ \arg\max\bar{\mathcal{C}} with 𝒟 1 \mathcal{D}_{1} , 𝒟 2 \mathcal{D}_{2} , and 𝒟 J ​ S \mathcal{D}_{JS} and with temperatures 0.5 0.5 and 2 2 ; arg ⁡ max ⁡ V \arg\max V ; the nine Label Wave configurations; and the rule based on the maximum of H ⁡ ( y ^ ∣ y ~ ) H(\hat{y}\mid\tilde{y}) . The association between the complexity peak and a confidence of approximately 0.6 0.6 can therefore be examined only where confidence rises slowly, which in these experiments occurred at ρ ≥ 0.6 \rho\geq 0.6 .

Two further checks indicate that the mean confidence alone does not determine the peak. First, a model in which every sample has the same two-level distribution, with the observed mean confidence as its largest probability, predicts the peak when the mean confidence reaches 0.76. The predicted peak came later than the observed one: median epochs 22, 29 and 47 against 6.5, 20 and 31 at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 , 0.6 and 0.8 (both 4 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 ). Since 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} averages 𝒞 ⁡ ( p i ) \mathcal{C}(p_{i}) over samples with very different confidences, its maximum depends on the spread of the confidences, not only on their mean, which is consistent with a confidence of about 0.6, rather than 0.76, at the peak. Second, the median Spearman correlation between 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} and S ¯ \bar{S} over all epochs ranged from 0.99 0.99 to 1.00 1.00 for ρ ≤ 0.6 \rho\leq 0.6 , although this correlation was dominated by the decline after the peak. Over the first 2 ​ t ∗ ​ ( 𝒞 ¯ ) + 2 2t^{*}(\bar{\mathcal{C}})+2 epochs, the corresponding values were 0.73 0.73 , 0.04 0.04 , 0.08 0.08 , and − 0.36 -0.36 for ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , 0.4 0.4 , 0.6 0.6 , and 0.8 0.8 , respectively. These findings suggest that the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} reflects changes in the spread of per-sample confidences during training. At high ρ \rho , these changes coincided with memorization and could not be separated from it within our experimental design. At low ρ \rho , the peak occurred before memorization began.

We evaluated the time average of 𝒞 i \mathcal{C}_{i} over the first 50 epochs as a score for detecting corrupted samples (H6 and Figure 11 ). With the score direction fixed in advance, its AUROC decreased from 0.707 0.707 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 to 0.401 0.401 at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 . An AUROC below 0.5 0.5 indicates that the score tends to rank samples in the direction opposite to the one specified. The comparison with label-dependent baselines involves a difference in the information available to each method. While 𝒞 i \mathcal{C}_{i} and the other geometric features depend only on p i p_{i} , EL2N ( Paul et al., 2021 ) , mean loss, area under the margin ( Pleiss et al., 2020 ) , forgetting events ( Toneva et al., 2019 ) , and cartography statistics ( Swayamdipta et al., 2020 ) also use the noisy label y ~ i \tilde{y}_{i} . The best-performing baseline, EL2N, achieved AUROC values between 0.977 0.977 and 0.999 0.999 when computed over the first 10 epochs, following Paul et al. (2021) . This difference in available information should be considered when interpreting the pre-specified non-inferiority comparison. Across the 60 runs included in the pre-specified analysis, the aggregate difference was Δ ​ AUROC = − 0.318 \Delta\mathrm{AUROC}=-0.318 . This analysis included SU and PERM at ρ = 1 \rho=1 , for which both scores performed at chance level. When the comparison was restricted to UI noise with 0 < ρ < 1 0<\rho<1 , the difference was Δ ​ AUROC = − 0.481 \Delta\mathrm{AUROC}=-0.481 .

A comparison with more closely matched information requirements is provided by simple label-free scores computed from the same predictions (Table 12 ). These comprise entropy, the largest predicted probability, and the margin between the two largest probabilities, each averaged over epochs; the temporal variance of p t ​ ( k ∣ x i ) p_{t}(k\mid x_{i}) , averaged over classes; and the fraction of consecutive epochs in which the predicted class changed. Over the first 50 epochs, temporal variance achieved the highest AUROC among these scores at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , with a value of 0.969 0.969 , compared with 0.707 0.707 for the time-averaged complexity. At ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 , the prediction-change score performed best, with an AUROC of 0.659 0.659 , compared with 0.401 0.401 for time-averaged complexity. With the pre-specified direction, time-averaged complexity had an AUROC below 0.5 0.5 in all ten seeds for ρ ≥ 0.6 \rho\geq 0.6 over the 50-epoch window, and for ρ ≥ 0.4 \rho\geq 0.4 over the 10 and 25-epoch windows. These results suggest that its usefulness as a ranking score depended in part on the noise rate and the observation window. Allowing the direction to be chosen retrospectively, as in the symmetric AUROC, resulted in values ranging from 0.53 0.53 to 0.71 0.71 . Even with this adjustment, complexity remained below the best label-free score for every window and noise rate considered. The differences were small, however, for the 10-epoch window at ρ ≥ 0.6 \rho\geq 0.6 , ranging from 0.002 0.002 to 0.004 0.004 .

For reference, the loss computed with the noisy labels achieved AUROC values between 0.977 0.977 and 0.999 0.999 over the first 10 epochs, when little memorization had occurred. Its discrimination was weaker over the 50-epoch window, with an AUROC of 0.722 0.722 at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 . Over the first 10 epochs, EL2N and noisy-label loss produced nearly identical rankings, with absolute per-run AUROC differences no greater than 0.001 0.001 . This similarity is consistent with both scores depending primarily on the probability assigned to the noisy label. chunks.section: 5.9 Robustness across datasets, noise models and optimizers (exploratory)
chunks.text: The results above come from one dataset, a family of symmetric noise models, and one optimizer. The 280 extension runs vary these factors in turn while retaining the architecture. Table 13 summarizes the results alongside those of the main grid.

In every condition, the identities held with residuals ≤ 1.2 × 10 − 14 \leq 1.2\times 10^{-14} . The fraction of scheduled test epochs within the 95th percentile of the null ranged from 89% to 97% across conditions, a descriptive result subject to the caveats in Section 5.4 . The median Spearman correlation between M M and ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} ranged from 0.977 to 1.000 across conditions with 0 < ρ < 1 0<\rho<1 (soft and hard versions). At the final epoch, the signal term deviated from its reference value by at most 0.014 in any run, except under weight decay (0.032 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 ), where predictions remained softer (Figure 12 ). SGD reached interpolation in all its runs (median epoch 113-122 for ρ > 0 \rho>0 ), and the cosine schedule reached interpolation at ρ ≤ 0.6 \rho\leq 0.6 . In those runs, the memorization term also reached its reference value: for example, 0.408 against 0.408 (cosine, ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , soft), and 0.970 (soft) and 0.980 (hard) against 0.980 (SGD, ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 ). As with the signal term, this is a sanity check of Proposition 4 . Training with Adam for 400 epochs did not lead to interpolation at ρ ∈ { 0.8 , 1 } \rho\in\{0.8,1\} : M M reached 0.975 and 0.978, and the soft memorization term reached 0.893 and 0.874, compared with 0.846 and 0.821 at epoch 200. The first 200 epochs of these runs were identical to the corresponding protocol runs, as expected under deterministic training.

The decomposition of Observation 1 held to 10 − 16 10^{-16} , and the share of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} contributed by corrupted samples at its peak remained close to the corrupted fraction (0.20, 0.38, 0.57 and 0.79 on Fashion-MNIST). Under UI noise, the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} occurred later as ρ \rho increased, whereas the best test epoch occurred earlier, in every training variant and on Fashion-MNIST (Table 13 , Figure 13 ). Under pair-flip noise, where at most 40% of labels were corrupted and confidence rose quickly, the peak occurred at epoch 1 (median) at every rate on MNIST and at epochs 1 and 2 on Fashion-MNIST, so its correlation with ρ \rho was weak ( r s = − 0.22 r_{s}=-0.22 and 0.27 0.27 , Table 13 ). The trend of the peak with ρ \rho observed under UI noise therefore did not carry over to pair-flip noise. The peak of V V was less regular: with SGD at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 , it occurred at epoch 1 in six runs and at epochs 53-60 in the other four, so its median in Figure 13 falls at epoch 1.

The ranking observed on the main grid held across all conditions (Table 13 , Figure 14 ). Averaged over 0 < ρ < 1 0<\rho<1 , noisy validation with 1000 samples and Label Wave incurred losses of 0.3-2.0 percentage points. Stopping at the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} incurred losses of 19-26 percentage points under UI noise, mostly at high ρ \rho , and 4-5 percentage points under pair-flip noise.

H7 predicted that, once the network had interpolated and its training predictions had become sharp, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} would no longer distinguish noisy from clean runs. Here, discrimination is measured by the AUROC between runs with ρ = 0 \rho=0 and runs with ρ > 0 \rho>0 , using the run-level 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} computed on the training set. With SGD, the AUROC was 1.00 1.00 both at the interpolation epoch and at epoch 200 for each noise rate considered (Figure 15 ). At epoch 200, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} ranged from 3.9 × 10 − 3 3.9\times 10^{-3} at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 to 8.0 × 10 − 3 8.0\times 10^{-3} at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 , compared with 4.0 × 10 − 4 4.0\times 10^{-4} for clean labels. This comparison is confounded by training time: the median interpolation epoch was 18 18 for clean SGD runs, whereas it ranged from 113 113 to 122 122 for noisy runs.

When runs were compared at matched times after interpolation, between 20 and 80 epochs, the ratio of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} in noisy runs to that in clean runs ranged from 2.4 2.4 to 4.3 4.3 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and from 5.3 5.3 to 9.2 9.2 at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 . The corresponding ratios at equal training epochs were 9.9 9.9 and 20 20 . The AUROC remained 1.00 1.00 throughout the matched-time comparison, although only 4 runs at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and 6 runs at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 reached 80 epochs after interpolation. Matching runs by training loss on the observed labels, at loss levels of 0.03 0.03 , 0.01 0.01 , or 0.003 0.003 , further reduced the ratio to values between 1.2 1.2 and 1.8 1.8 , while the AUROC remained between 0.97 0.97 and 1.00 1.00 . These loss levels were reached at substantially different training times: between epochs 11 11 and 30 30 in clean runs and between epochs 88 88 and 200 200 in noisy runs. No noisy run reached a loss of 0.001 0.001 . Thus, neither comparison fully removes the effect of training time. Corrupted samples retained complexity values between 8 × 10 − 3 8\times 10^{-3} and 9 × 10 − 3 9\times 10^{-3} at every noise rate. Clean samples within noisy runs also retained higher complexity than samples in clean runs, with values of 2.6 × 10 − 3 2.6\times 10^{-3} at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and 7.3 × 10 − 3 7.3\times 10^{-3} at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 . Within the training horizon considered, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} therefore continued to separate noisy from clean runs after interpolation, although training time could not be fully matched. After interpolation, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} decreased in both groups, with a proportionally faster decline in clean runs. Consequently, the absolute difference narrowed while the ratio increased. The budget in Proposition 2 is an accounting device built from standard identities. Several of our checks confirm the implementation rather than the measure: the identities (H1), the Fano bound and the end point hold by construction, and on held-out data the null holds by construction, where the permutation test rejected slightly more often than its nominal level. The empirical content is narrower. On the training set, ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} rose together with M M (H2 and H3) and reached its complete-memorization value in runs that interpolated, while its held-out counterpart stayed near zero. Two qualifications are important. First, in the regimes studied, ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} was close to what the training accuracies on clean and corrupted samples imply, and within a run it was close to a monotone function of M M . Its practical advantage over the raw memorized fraction is mainly the absence of a chance level, which mattered most at ρ = 1 \rho=1 and under pair-flip noise and which a chance-corrected κ \kappa also largely removes. Second, ℳ I \mathcal{M}_{I} measures a different notion from counterfactual memorization ( Feldman and Zhang, 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) : it is a property of the whole prediction map rather than the influence of a sample on its own prediction. Relating these notions and testing the null on held-out training samples rather than the test set are natural next steps. The term is a function-space counterpart of the label-noise information in the weights studied by Harutyunyan et al. (2020) , although we do not claim a formal relation. Because it requires clean labels, we used it as a reference quantity rather than a diagnostic.

Under complete UI corruption, the training labels are complementary labels, and the network learned from them: test accuracy fell below chance while the predictions retained information about the true class, unlike under SU and PERM . Full UI corruption is therefore not a substitute for random labels in our setting.

No pre-specified hypothesis addressed this question, and the following reading is exploratory. 𝒞 ⁡ ( p ) \mathcal{C}(p) is non-monotone in the confidence of p p , and the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} occurred when the confidences of the training samples passed through an intermediate range. At low noise this happened before memorization began. At high noise it happened during memorization, close to the epoch at which the mean confidence reached about 0.6, and our design cannot separate the rise in confidence from memorization there. On clean labels and under pair-flip noise, confidence rose within the first epochs and the peak occurred at epochs 1-2, which per-epoch logging cannot resolve. A model with homogeneous confidence did not predict the peak, which suggests that the spread of confidences matters. This reading is consistent with the shift in peak time with ρ \rho under UI noise, with its sensitivity to temperature (H9), and with stopping at the peak working at low noise and failing at high noise (H5 and the comparison with established rules). The pre-specified expectation that V V and the label-free heterogeneity term would mark the memorization phase (H4) was supported only for V V , and only in a weak sense, because the phase spans many epochs. After interpolation, 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} still distinguished noisy from clean runs within the observed horizon, contrary to H7, also at matched training loss although by a smaller factor, possibly through residual uncertainty on corrupted samples. The centroid trajectories in the entropy-disequilibrium plane were not stable across seeds relative to the separation between corruption rates (H10) and did not reveal the heterogeneity of the predictions (Appendix A ). In our runs, the plane added little beyond the per-sample summaries. As decision tools, the established methods included in our comparisons performed better at high noise (H5 and H6).

The study used one architecture, a multilayer perceptron, and two small image datasets. It considered only synthetic class-conditional noise (Assumption 1 ). Instance-dependent noise violates the assumption underlying Proposition 3 , in which case the memorization term may also capture learnable patterns in the noise. Under the pre-specified protocol (Adam with a constant learning rate), no corrupted run reached interpolation. Interpolation and H7 could therefore be studied only post hoc, on SGD and cosine-schedule runs, with approximately 80 epochs of training after interpolation. The extension was defined after the main results and is exploratory. On Fashion-MNIST at ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 , M M reached 0.9 in only one of 10 runs, so t 90 t_{90} is censored in that condition. Furthermore, Label Wave was re-implemented from its description rather than the authors’ code; the conclusion that the peak of 𝒞 ¯ \bar{\mathcal{C}} was outperformed at high noise also holds against noisy validation, which does not depend on this re-implementation. The selection of a label-free rule used clean labels on the validation half, and selection with noisy validation labels was not evaluated. Progressive early stopping ( Bai et al., 2021 ) and counterfactual memorization were not evaluated. The hypotheses were fixed in an internal protocol, not in a public registry, and some criteria turned out to be lenient (H3, H4 and H5) or very hard to meet (H6 and H10). In the main grid the noise seed was tied to the initialization seed. Finally, plug-in information estimates are biased in finite samples; we addressed this using permutation nulls (Section 5.4 ).

We asked how much information about label noise a classifier’s predictions reflect and how it relates to accuracy-based measures of memorization (RQ1), and what statistical complexity tracks during training and whether it is useful as a tool (RQ2). Of the ten pre-specified hypotheses, five were supported, four were not, and one could not be tested under the protocol. For RQ1, standard information identities decompose the information in a classifier’s predictions into signal, memorization and heterogeneity terms. In our experiments, the in-sample memorization term rose with the memorized fraction while its held-out counterpart stayed near zero, but it was close to what the training accuracies already implied; its main advantage over the raw memorized fraction, the absence of a chance level, could largely be recovered through chance correction. Under complete corruption with incorrect labels, the network learned from the complementary labels and reached below-chance test accuracy, so in our runs this form of corruption was not equivalent to random labels.

For RQ2, the peak of the mean statistical complexity preceded memorization at low noise and occurred during memorization at high noise, close to the epoch at which the mean training confidence reached about 0.6; confidence and memorization could not be separated there. In our comparisons, mean complexity was not competitive as a stopping rule at high noise, nor as a detector of corrupted samples. An exploratory extension to Fashion-MNIST, pair-flip noise and four training variants gave similar results under uniform noise, although under pair-flip noise the complexity peak occurred within the first two epochs. These conclusions are limited to one architecture, two small datasets and synthetic noise; their applicability to convolutional architectures, larger datasets and real label noise remains to be tested.

Label Wave ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) monitors the fraction of training samples whose predicted class changes between consecutive evaluations, smooths it with a trailing moving average over the last k k evaluations, and stops once the smoothed value has failed to improve on its running minimum for p p consecutive evaluations; the selected epoch is that of the minimum. In our re-implementation, the evaluation interval is one epoch and the predictions are computed on the full training set (Section 4 ).
